## DI-0301 reaches its last system: one donor, three locations

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is back with the capstone piece of **DI-0301**, her data-integrity
self-assessment. DED-0458 is settled except for "accurate," left open on purpose. Fairview's paper
donor file is settled as its own record of record. LAB-07 has a genuine, fixable gap on documented
fitness-for-use evidence. Today she's not looking at one record or one instrument — she's looking
at whether Lakeshore's three locations agree about the same donor.

Here's the system she's testing. Lakeshore runs a central site plus two satellite collection sites,
Brookfield and Fairview. A donor can walk into any of the three. Each location needs to know, before
it ever draws blood, whether that specific donor is currently eligible to donate anywhere in the
system — not just at the location they happen to be standing in. If a donor was turned away at
Fairview last week, Brookfield has to know that too, or the whole point of turning them away at
Fairview evaporates.

She builds a timeline to test it, not a hypothetical. Picture a donor who gives at Fairview on an
ordinary collection day. Routine post-donation testing on that unit comes back reactive for one of
the transfusion-transmitted infections Lakeshore screens every donation for — a result generic
enough that it doesn't need a specific diagnosis named here, just the fact that it's the kind of
reactive result that triggers a donor deferral under Lakeshore's standard procedures. Fairview's own
staff do exactly what you'd expect: they flag that donor, locally, the same day the result comes
back. If that same donor tried to walk back into Fairview next week, Fairview's own front-desk check
would catch it immediately.

Here's her actual question, the one this whole module exists to answer: if that same donor instead
drove to Brookfield, or showed up at the central site, the week after being deferred at Fairview —
would *they* catch it too? And if the honest answer is "not necessarily, not right away" — how long
is "not right away," really? No citations yet. Just a donor, three locations, and a question your QA
thinks nobody at Lakeshore has actually sat down and answered out loud.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module exists to head off. A deferral that works perfectly at the location
where it happened, and means nothing anywhere else in the system, isn't really a deferral at all —
it's a local note. The entire point of deferring a donor is that the donor, not just the paperwork
at one address, is the thing being restricted. If Lakeshore's locations don't actually share that
restriction promptly, a donor can be simultaneously "deferred" at Fairview and "eligible" at
Brookfield, which is a contradiction a computer system can hold without complaint and a patient
cannot survive without risk.

You already own the ITSM (IT service management) concept this needs, even if you've never had to
treat it as a patient-safety question before. Every organization running a **CMDB** (configuration
management database) across multiple regional offices has faced the same design problem: when a
central system and several remote sites each hold their own copy of the same data, there's always a
window where they can briefly disagree before replication catches up. The term of art for that is
**eventual consistency** — a concept from distributed systems. It doesn't promise zero delay between
one site updating a fact and every other site seeing it. It promises the system *eventually*
converges on the same answer everywhere, and the real engineering question is never "can we make the
delay zero" (usually impossible, or absurdly expensive to get close to) — it's "is our actual delay
small enough for what's riding on it."

Here's where the regulated world demands more. For an ordinary CMDB, a brief window where one
regional office sees an asset's old owner or an outdated patch level is an inconvenience — mildly
annoying, rarely urgent, because nothing catastrophic happens in that window. For a cumulative
deferred-donor record, that same kind of window is a direct patient-safety exposure. A donor who
shouldn't be accepted anywhere in the system can, for a real stretch of time, still show up as
eligible somewhere in it — and "briefly," here, can mean something much longer than it ever would
for a spreadsheet.

## The rule in plain English

Two different regulatory ideas are doing the work in this module, and they build on each other.

**First: every unit of blood has to trace back to one donor, provably, forever.** That's the job of
a donor number — a unique identifier assigned to each accepted donor that links the unit collected,
the donor's own medical record, every component or product made from that unit, and every record
describing what ultimately happened to those products. Without that link, "this donor is deferred"
and "this unit came from that donor" are two facts with no reliable way to connect them. The donor
number is the thread that makes everything else in this module possible.

**Second: keeping one donor's eligibility consistent across Lakeshore's locations is two separate
obligations, not one.** The first obligation is purely local: each location — Fairview, Brookfield,
the central site — has to maintain its own record of every donor found ineligible or deferred *at
that location*, specifically so that location never collects from, or releases blood from, a donor
who's currently deferred there. That part is immediate, by design — it's what let Fairview's own
staff catch the same donor on the spot if they walked back in next week.

The second obligation is system-wide: Lakeshore has to maintain, across every location operating
under the same license or common management, a **cumulative** record of donors deferred specifically
because a donation tested reactive for one of a named set of transfusion-transmitted infections.
That cumulative record is what Brookfield and the central site would actually consult to catch a
donor deferred somewhere else. And the regulation sets a specific floor for how often that cumulative
record has to be refreshed: **at least monthly.**

Sit with that phrase for a second, because it's the sharpest point in this whole module. "At least
monthly" is a regulatory floor — the minimum frequency the rule requires. Meeting it exactly, updating
no more than once a month, no faster, is **fully compliant with the regulation's letter.** It can
also, at the very same time, leave open a real window — up to just under a month, in the worst case,
if a deferral happens right after a monthly update cycle runs — during which a donor deferred at one
site could, in principle, still be accepted at a different one. Compliant and risky aren't opposites
here. They can both be true of the exact same practice, and the regulation itself doesn't resolve
which is more important to you. That's Lakeshore's own risk tolerance to decide, not something
606.160(e) decides for you — the kind of judgment this curriculum's `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`
foundation and `quality-risk-management` gave you the vocabulary for already, applied here to a
donor-safety question instead of a deviation or a change.

There's one more piece, easy to forget: the cumulative record isn't supposed to only ever grow. A
donor who was deferred can, under the right circumstances, later be requalified — found eligible to
donate again. When that happens, the cumulative record has to be revised to remove them, or Lakeshore
ends up turning away donors it has no current reason to turn away. Keeping the list accurate means
keeping it current in both directions, not just adding to it.

A donor number must link the unit collected to the donor, the donor's medical record, any component or product from that unit, and all records of history and disposition. | The identity thread that has to hold across BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software), Fairview's paper file, and every other Lakeshore system, so "this donor" means the same donor everywhere. |

Each location must maintain its own record of donors found ineligible or deferred at that location, to prevent collecting from or releasing blood from a currently deferred donor there. | What Fairview already does, immediately, the day its own reactive result comes back. |

All locations under the same license or common management must maintain a cumulative record of donors deferred under § 610.41 for a reactive test under § 610.40(a)(1) (HIV — human immunodeficiency virus; HBV — hepatitis B virus; HCV — hepatitis C virus) or, outside Source Plasma establishments, § 610.40(a)(2) (HTLV — human T-lymphotropic virus; Chagas disease). | The system-wide list Brookfield and the central site would actually consult to catch a donor deferred at Fairview. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(e)(3) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph e, sub-three" | Regulation. The cumulative record must be updated **at least monthly** to add newly deferred donors. | The regulatory floor DI-0301 tests against the worked timeline below — the sharpest finding in this module. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(e)(4) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph e, sub-four" | Regulation. The cumulative record must be revised to remove donors requalified under § 610.41(b). | Keeps the system-wide list honest in both directions — not a one-way ratchet. |
| 21 CFR 610.41 (named only, not quoted — not independently saved in `sources/`) | "six-ten point forty-one" | Regulation, governing donor deferral itself. 606.160(e) cites it as the authority under which a donor is actually deferred. | The rule that makes a reactive test result into an actual deferral decision, one step before 606.160(e)'s recordkeeping duty applies. |
| 21 CFR 610.40 (named only, not quoted — not independently saved in `sources/`) | "six-ten point forty" | Regulation, governing test requirements. 606.160(e) cites its paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) as the specific reactive results that trigger a § 610.41 deferral landing on the cumulative record. | What makes the Fairview donor's result the kind of reactive finding 606.160(e)(2) actually tracks. |

## The actual text

Start with the donor-number requirement, quoted in full, verbatim, from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`:

> (c) A donor number shall be assigned to each accepted donor, which relates the unit of blood
> collected to that donor, to his medical record, to any component or blood product from that
> donor's unit of blood, and to all records describing the history and ultimate disposition of these
> products.

Read that sentence as a chain, link by link: donor number → unit → medical record → every component
or product made from that unit → every record of what happened to those products afterward. Module 3
already settled that Fairview's paper file, not its BECS re-entry, is the documented record of record
for Fairview's own donor-eligibility determination. That decision doesn't touch this one. Whichever
format is authoritative, the donor number still has to be the thread tying the paper file, the BECS
entry, and every downstream product record back to one specific person — not a name that might be
spelled two different ways, not a date of birth someone mistypes once. One number, one donor, every
record, everywhere.

Now the full text of paragraph (e), "Records of deferred donors," verbatim from the same source —
this course's first full treatment of this paragraph, and its central regulatory floor:

> (e) *Records of deferred donors.* (1) Establishments must maintain at each location a record of all
> donors found to be ineligible or deferred at that location so that blood and blood components from
> an ineligible donor are not collected and/or released while the donor is ineligible or deferred;
> and
>
> (2) Establishments must maintain at all locations operating under the same license or under common
> management a cumulative record of donors deferred from donation under § 610.41 of this chapter
> because their donation tested reactive under § 610.40(a)(1) of this chapter for evidence of
> infection due to HIV, HBV, or HCV. In addition, establishments other than Source Plasma
> establishments must include in this cumulative record donors deferred from donation under § 610.41
> of this chapter because their donation tested reactive under § 610.40(a)(2) of this chapter for
> evidence of infection due to HTLV or Chagas disease.
>
> (3) The cumulative record described in paragraph (e)(2) of this section must be updated at least
> monthly to add donors newly deferred under § 610.41 of this chapter due to reactive tests for
> evidence of infection due to HIV, HBV, or HCV, and, if applicable, HTLV or Chagas disease.
>
> (4) Establishments must revise the cumulative record described in paragraph (e)(2) of this section
> to remove donors who have been requalified under § 610.41(b) of this chapter.

Four numbered paragraphs, four distinct duties. (e)(1) is purely local — Fairview's own problem to
solve, on its own, the day it happens. (e)(2) defines the cumulative record and exactly which
deferrals have to be on it: ones driven by a reactive test under 610.40(a)(1) — HIV, HBV
(hepatitis B virus), or HCV (hepatitis C virus) — for every establishment, plus, for establishments
that aren't Source Plasma collection facilities like Lakeshore, reactive tests under 610.40(a)(2) for
HTLV (human T-lymphotropic virus) or Chagas disease. (e)(3) sets the clock: at least monthly. (e)(4)
is the one easiest to forget — the cumulative record has to come back down, not just go up, when a
donor is requalified.

HIV, HBV, HCV, HTLV, and Chagas disease are named here exactly as 606.160(e) itself names them — this
module isn't diagnosing anyone or inventing clinical detail beyond what the regulation's own text
already states. 610.41 and 610.40 aren't independently saved in `sources/` for this curriculum, so
this module names them, exactly as 606.160(e) cites them, and doesn't quote their own content: 610.41
is the regulation that actually governs donor deferral and requalification; 610.40 is the regulation
that sets the test requirements whose reactive results are what trigger a 610.41 deferral in the
first place. 606.160(e) is the recordkeeping duty sitting on top of both — it assumes a 610.41
deferral has already happened and tells Lakeshore how to record and share it.

### Walking the Fairview timeline through the text

Here's DI-0301's worked scenario, this time with the citations attached.

**The day of the reactive result.** Fairview's donor gives blood. Routine testing on that unit comes
back reactive under 610.40(a)(1) or (a)(2) — again, generically, the kind of result 606.160(e)(2)
names, not a specific diagnosis invented for this lesson. Under 610.41, that result drives a
deferral. The moment that happens, 606.160(e)(1) is the rule in motion: Fairview has to maintain its
own local record of that deferral, specifically so Fairview itself doesn't collect from or release
blood from that donor again while the deferral stands. In practice, that's immediate — the same day,
built into Fairview's own front-desk check. If this exact donor walked back into Fairview next week,
Fairview would catch it, full stop. That part of the system works exactly as designed, and it's worth
noticing precisely why: it's local, so nothing has to travel anywhere for it to work.

**The gap.** Now ask what has to happen for Brookfield, or the central site, to catch the same
donor. Neither one has its own first-hand record of a deferral that happened at Fairview. The only
way either of them finds out is through the cumulative record 606.160(e)(2) requires across all of
Lakeshore's locations — and that record, per (e)(3), only has to be updated **at least monthly.**

Here's the honest, bounded way to state the exposure, without inventing a false-precise number: if
Fairview's deferral happens the day *after* a monthly update cycle has just run, that donor's
deferral sits unreflected in the cumulative record until the next cycle comes around — up to just
under a month later, in the worst case. During that entire window, if the donor drove to Brookfield
or to the central site and tried to donate again, nothing in the cumulative record they'd check would
stop them. Lakeshore would be meeting 606.160(e)(3) to the letter the entire time. Nothing described
here is a violation. It's a real, bounded gap sitting inside full compliance — which is exactly why
it's worth taking seriously rather than dismissing because "the regulation doesn't require anything
faster."

This is the same shape of question `csv-and-becs` module 7 raised once, in a different register: how
fast a status change at one Lakeshore location actually reaches another over the BECS-to-satellite
interface, the quarantine-propagation-latency question that module built for a unit's quarantine
status. This module's subject — a donor's deferral status propagating across sites — is a close
cousin, but the stakes and the lens are different: that was an interface-validation question about
proving data arrives complete, correct, on time. This is a data-governance and patient-safety question
about whether the regulatory floor itself is fast enough. One sentence of callback is all that
deserves — the two questions rhyme, they aren't the same question.

### DI-0301's recommendation to you

Here's where your QA brings DI-0301's capstone finding to you directly, instead of leaving it as an
open question for someone else to pick up. Her finding, stated plainly: Lakeshore's cumulative
deferred-donor record is fully compliant, meeting 606.160(e)(3)'s "at least monthly" floor every
cycle, with the dated log to prove it. And the worst-case gap her timeline exposes — up to just under
a month between a deferral at one site and the cumulative record catching up everywhere else — is
real, not hypothetical, and not something the regulation itself asks Lakeshore to close.

Her recommendation: consider updating the cumulative record more frequently than the monthly floor
requires. Not because 606.160(e) demands it — it doesn't, and she's careful to say so in her own
write-up, the same way this course has flagged every other "this is not a regulatory requirement"
moment. This is a risk-based, industry-practice judgment, squarely in the territory
`risk-and-controls-vocabulary` and `quality-risk-management` already gave you the tools for: weigh a
real exposure against a real cost, and decide deliberately, rather than defaulting to the floor
because nobody asked the question.

And she states the cost honestly, instead of making faster updates sound free. A more frequent
cumulative-record refresh means more load on whatever system reconciles the three locations' records,
more staff time actually running and verifying each cycle, and more coordination overhead keeping
Brookfield, Fairview, and the central site synchronized on a tighter schedule than the regulation
requires. None of that is free, and pretending it is would make this recommendation dishonest in the
other direction. What she's not doing is naming a specific number — not "update weekly," not "update
daily" — as the obviously correct answer. That number is yours to set, weighing the cost against how
much of that worst-case window you're willing to tolerate. Her job was to surface the tradeoff
clearly enough that you can actually make that call. That's exactly what a good self-assessment
recommendation looks like: a real finding, an honest cost, and a decision left where it belongs.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor
wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has a multi-site governance policy. They'd ask for specific, dated
proof, at each of the four duties above.

**For 606.160(e)(1):** evidence that Fairview, Brookfield, and the central site each maintain their
own local deferred-donor record, and that each location's own check actually runs before collection
— not an assumption that "the system would catch it." A bad answer sounds like "we'd know." A good
answer shows the local record and the specific check step that consults it.

**For 606.160(e)(2) and (e)(3):** a dated log of cumulative-record updates, showing the actual
interval between them — genuinely monthly or faster, not "roughly" monthly with gaps that stretch
longer some cycles. A bad answer sounds like "we update it regularly." A good answer produces the
update history and lets the inspector do the arithmetic.

**For 606.160(e)(4):** evidence that requalified donors are actually being removed from the
cumulative record, not just added to in one direction indefinitely. A list that only ever grows is
itself a finding.

**For the risk question this module's whole scenario turns on:** whether Lakeshore has ever actually
asked, and documented an answer to, whether monthly is fast enough for its own risk tolerance — not
whether the regulation requires anything faster, because it doesn't. An inspector reading a self-
assessment like DI-0301's would likely see an honest answer to that question as a sign of a
functioning quality system, not a confession of a violation.

## Common traps

**"The local record at each site is enough — the cumulative record is just a backstop."** Backwards.
606.160(e)(1)'s local record is what stops a donor from being re-collected at the *same* site where
they were deferred. It does nothing for any other site. The cumulative record under (e)(2) is the
only mechanism that lets Brookfield or the central site learn about a deferral that happened at
Fairview at all. Treating the cumulative record as a lesser, secondary control gets the architecture
backwards: it's the only piece doing cross-site work, and it's the piece bound by the slower,
monthly-floor update cycle.

**"Lakeshore updates the cumulative record every month, so the multi-site system is as safe as it
needs to be."** Not necessarily — and this is **not something 606.160(e) itself resolves.** Updating
at least monthly satisfies the regulation's letter completely. Whether monthly is fast enough that a
deferred donor's window of apparent eligibility elsewhere in the system is an acceptable risk is a
separate question, and it's Lakeshore's own risk-based judgment to make, not a box the regulation
checks for you. Confusing "compliant" with "as safe as it should be" is exactly the gap this module
exists to name.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask to see the dated update history for the cumulative deferred-donor record, not a policy
  statement that it's updated monthly.** A policy that says "monthly" and a log that shows it
  happening are different kinds of evidence, the same distinction this course has drawn before for
  audit trails and password revision.
- **Ask whether anyone has ever calculated, honestly, the worst-case gap between a deferral at one
  site and the cumulative record reaching the others** — and treat "we've never actually worked that
  out" as the finding, not a reason to assume it's fine.
- **Push for a documented answer on update cadence, one way or the other.** Either Lakeshore
  consciously accepts the monthly floor as sufficient for this specific risk, or it decides to go
  faster. What's not acceptable is never having asked the question at all — the same "nobody decided"
  pattern this course has flagged before, now applied to a patient-safety-adjacent cadence instead of
  an audit-trail review schedule.
- **Confirm the donor-number link (606.160(c)) actually survives across formats** — Fairview's paper
  file, its BECS reporting copy, and the central cumulative record all have to resolve to the same
  donor, by the same number, every time. A donor-number mismatch between formats is a worse version
  of the same ambiguity module 3 found at Fairview, now with cross-site consequences.
- **If you do decide to recommend a faster cadence, cost it honestly** — more frequent updates mean
  more system load, more staff time reconciling records, more coordination between three locations,
  not just a settings change. A risk-based decision made without naming its own cost isn't really a
  decision; it's a hope.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: A donor is deferred at Fairview this morning. Does Fairview have to wait for the next monthly cumulative-record update before it can refuse that same donor if they try to donate at Fairview again next week?

No. 21 CFR 606.160(e)(1) requires each location to maintain its own local record of donors found
ineligible or deferred *at that location*, specifically so blood isn't collected from or released
from an ineligible donor there. That obligation is immediate and purely local — it doesn't depend on
the cumulative record at all. The monthly update cadence in (e)(3) governs the separate, system-wide
cumulative record under (e)(2), which is what Brookfield or the central site would need to catch the
same donor. Fairview itself should never need to wait for that cycle to protect its own collections.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Lakeshore updates its cumulative deferred-donor record exactly once a month, on schedule, every time. Is that fully compliant with 606.160(e)(3)? And does that mean the multi-site system is as safe as it needs to be?

Compliant, yes — "at least monthly" is the regulation's own floor, and meeting it exactly, with a
real, verifiable monthly cadence, satisfies 606.160(e)(3)'s letter completely. Safe enough is a
different question, and **this is not something 606.160(e) answers for you** — it's a genuine
industry-practice, risk-based judgment call. A donor deferred right after a monthly update cycle runs
could, in the worst case, go unreflected in the cumulative record for up to just under a month, during
which a different Lakeshore location could accept them. Whether that window is an acceptable risk, or
one worth closing with a faster update cadence, is Lakeshore's own risk tolerance to set — the
regulation sets the floor; choosing to go faster is a risk-based decision, not a regulatory mandate,
and the two questions ("are we compliant" and "are we safe enough") can have different honest answers
at the exact same time.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Module 3 settled Fairview's paper donor file as its own record of record, with its BECS entry as a documented reporting copy only. Given that, does 606.160(c)'s donor-number requirement still apply to Fairview's donor records?

Yes, and this is worth getting exactly right — which format is the record of record and whether the
donor-number link has to hold are two separate questions. 606.160(c) requires a donor number linking
the unit, the donor, their medical record, any component or product from that unit, and every record
of its history and disposition — and that requirement doesn't care which artifact Lakeshore has
designated as authoritative. Fairview's paper file being the record of record (module 3's finding)
means the paper file is what Fairview relies on and protects as the real record. It doesn't exempt
Fairview from making sure the same donor number appears, correctly, on the paper file, on its BECS
reporting copy, and on any product record derived from that donor's unit. A donor-number mismatch
between the paper file and its own reporting copy would be its own, separate finding — not resolved
by, and not excused by, module 3's record-of-record decision.
:::

## Where this goes next

This closes `data-integrity-and-records`, and DI-0301 reaches the end of its first full pass across
Lakeshore's systems. It's worth looking back at the shape of the whole course, because none of its six
modules stood alone. Module 1 gave you ALCOA (attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded,
original or a true copy, accurate) as something you test letter by letter, not read off a record's
surface — and drew the line between that, FDA's own term, and "ALCOA+," industry practice layered on
top of it. Module 2 gave audit trails and e-signatures their first real depth in this curriculum: who
has to review an audit trail, how often, and the five specific controls — 11.50, 11.70, 11.100,
11.200, 11.300 — an e-signature actually has to clear to stand in for ink. Module 3 finally defined
*predicate rule*, the term this curriculum had named but never explained, and used it to decide which
format of a record — paper or electronic — Lakeshore actually relies on, for DED-0458 and for
Fairview both. Module 4 applied FDA's own four-part legacy-system test to LAB-07, a real instrument
with a real, fixable gap. Module 5 went past 606.160(d)'s product-record clock to the records that
don't share its schedule, and caught a disaster-recovery snapshot being called something it isn't.
And this module closed the loop across Lakeshore's locations: one donor number, meant to mean the
same thing everywhere, and a monthly floor that's fully compliant and still worth a second look.

Some things this course deliberately leaves open, and that's not a loose end — it's an honest
self-assessment doing its job. DED-0458's "accurate" ALCOA letter is still unresolved, exactly as
module 1 left it. LAB-07's documented-fitness-for-use gap is still a real, standing finding, not
quietly closed here for the sake of a tidy ending. The donor-record retention-clock question module 5
raised is still routed to document control, not answered by assumption. A self-assessment's job is to
surface findings accurately, not to manufacture a clean résumé by the time the project wraps — DI-0301
did its job precisely by leaving these open rather than papering over them.

And two things stay out of this course entirely, on purpose, because they belong to courses this
curriculum hasn't built yet. Every system in DI-0301's path — BECS, the satellite sites' own
infrastructure, whatever eventually replaces LAB-07 — sits on vendor relationships this course never
evaluated as vendor relationships: the GRC (governance, risk, and compliance) and vendor-risk
questions a cloud or hosted record-keeping vendor actually raises belong to
`vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`, a future course. And every donor and patient record this
course has handled as a *data-integrity* object also carries its own privacy obligations — HIPAA
(Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) specifically — that this course never touched,
by design. That's `healthcare-security-and-privacy`'s subject, also still ahead.

You came into this course able to name Part 11 and ALCOA+ in passing, the way `csv-and-becs` left
them — real terms, pointed at, not yet yours. You leave it able to pull a record apart letter by
letter, defend or challenge an e-signature setup clause by clause, decide which format of a record
actually counts as the original, run FDA's own legacy-system test against a piece of equipment nobody
had questioned in years, catch a backup that isn't a backup, and ask the one question that ties all
six modules together: when this system tells you something about a donor, a record, or a unit, how do
you actually know it's telling the same site-to-site, format-to-format, person-to-person? That's the
finish line this course set out to reach — and it's yours now, not just DI-0301's.
